entries.text: Everyone in Chicago knows somebody. It was the thirtieth of December, a matinee, the house packed with mothers and children for the Christmas pantomime, when the scenery caught fire and the curtain did not come down and the doors opened inwards. Six hundred people died in a quarter of an hour. Mostly women and children.

entries.text: Everybody wants to go. It opened in April for the Louisiana Purchase, a hundred years of it, and they say it is bigger than our own Fair of ninety-three. There are villages of people from all over the world that you can walk through.

entries.text: A whole morning every week, two of us, with whiting and ammonia and soft cloths, in the butler's pantry with the door shut. Forks, spoons, salvers, candlesticks, the tea service, the epergne for the centre of the table. Every piece is counted out and counted back.

levels.8-10: A whole morning every week, for two of us. We use polish and soft cloths, in a little room by the dining room, with the door shut. We do the forks, spoons, trays, candlesticks, the tea set, and the big dish for the middle of the table. Every piece is counted out and counted back.

entries.text: The young ladies, calling each other about dances. Their mother says it is not ladylike to speak on the telephone. They do it anyway, in the back hall, in whispers, and I am to say they are out if their mother asks.

entries.text: A chicken pie that the master asks for every Sunday and is not supposed to have, because the doctor says he is too stout. On Sunday I make it anyway. The mistress pretends not to notice. Upstairs is full of things everyone pretends not to notice.

entries.text: The ice box, an oak chest lined with zinc, with a block of lake ice in the top that the ice man brings every morning, a hundred pounds on his back with tongs. entries.text: From the lakes and ponds north of the city, cut in the winter in great blocks and stored in ice houses packed in sawdust. In July the ice man is the most popular man on the Avenue. The children follow his wagon for the chips.

entries.text: Six in the stable behind the house: two pairs of carriage horses, bays, matched to the hair, a cob for the light trap, and the master's saddle horse that he does not ride as often as he should. entries.text: A brougham for the master in town, a victoria for the mistress on fine afternoons in the park, and a big closed carriage for the opera and the theatre. entries.text: We are a club. Every carriage house along the alley has a coachman, and we stand in the alley in the evening, smoking, and talk about horses and masters. We know whose horse is lame, whose groom drinks, and whose master is going broke before his banker does.

entries.text: Waiting. Outside the opera, outside a dinner, outside a ball, in January, on the box, with a buffalo robe and a lantern, until two in the morning. The horses stand with their blankets on and their breath smoking and I stand with them. You get to know a horse well on those nights.

entries.text: On my father's farm in Kerry, and then as a stable boy for an English family in Dublin, and then in the livery stables of New York, and then here. Twenty years of horses. I can tell a horse's age by its teeth and its temper by its ears, and a bad groom by the horse's coat.

entries.text: Steady nerves above all. A carriage horse in Chicago must stand still for cable cars, elevated trains, fire engines, brass bands and the motor cars. He must go at a walk among a thousand other horses without kicking any of them. A horse like that is worth more than a racehorse.

entries.text: Monday, every Monday, in the laundry in the basement, with three set tubs, a copper boiler on the range, a wringer, and a drying room with racks for when it rains. The whole house's linen, every sheet, napkin, collar and petticoat. Tuesday is ironing. Wednesday is mending.

entries.text: From six in the morning to six at night, two of us. The white things boiled, the coloured things in warm water, the woollens in cool, the master's collars starched stiff enough to cut a finger. By evening the steam has taken the curl out of my hair and the skin off my knuckles.

entries.text: Eleven years ago, in the summer of 1893, Chicago held the World's Columbian Exposition in Jackson Park, and the whole world came to see it. entries.text: I went forty times. Everybody did. People came from every country in the world and stood in the Court of Honour at night with their mouths open. They called it the White City. entries.text: Two years ago our firm and McCormick's and Deering's and the others came together into one company, the International Harvester, and I am a vice president of it. entries.text: Fourteen years ago a young minister named Dr. Gunsaulus preached a sermon called: What I would do with a million dollars. Afterwards he went up to the minister and said: if you will give five years of your life, I will give the million dollars.

entries.text: I came to Chicago in 1835, a boy of fifteen, with my father. It was a town of a few hundred people, frame houses and log cabins in the mud along the river, and the old fort, and the Potawatomi camped on the prairie. That summer the great land craze was on, and every man in Chicago was buying and selling lots that were under water half the year.

entries.text: I learned to speak a little of the Potawatomi language, trading with them. That autumn they gathered for the last time and went away west across the Mississippi, as the treaty said. I watched them go. Now I live on Prairie Avenue in a house of stone, on land that was open prairie when I was a boy, with wolves on it. I am one of the last who remember. When I am gone, nobody will.

entries.text: My father is General Stephen D. Lee, who commanded an army corps for the South in the war, and was at Vicksburg and Atlanta and Nashville. I grew up in Mississippi, in the years after the war, when we had nothing but our name. I studied law at Harvard and abroad, and came north to work for the Illinois Central Railroad, which runs from here all the way down to my father's country.

entries.text: I went to work for Mr. Philip Armour when I was a young man, and I have been in the packing business ever since. Every day the trains bring in cattle and hogs and sheep from the whole West, and every day we kill them and dress them and pack them and send them out in refrigerator cars to every city in the country, and to Europe.

entries.text: For many years I have been president of the Illinois Humane Society. We began by protecting horses, because the horses of this city are beaten and starved and worked until they drop in the street. Then we began to protect children, because, God help us, children in this city are treated worse than the horses.

entries.text: I am a doctor of the eye. I came to Chicago from Canada by way of Europe, where I studied in the great eye hospitals of London and Vienna and Berlin. Every day in my office men and women come to me afraid of going blind, and some of them I can help, and some I cannot.

entries.text: The eye is the most beautiful thing in the body, I think. When you look into it with the ophthalmoscope, with the little light, you see the blood vessels branching like the roots of a tree, and the nerve where the world comes in. When I am not in my office, I am watching birds. Every creature sees the world differently. I would like to know how.
